note: Starter set of question details with official web references. Apply on seed.

details.summary: NTSB Part 830 requires immediate notification for accidents involving substantial damage — damage that adversely affects structural strength, performance, or flight characteristics of the aircraft, and that normally requires major repair or replacement of the affected component. Cosmetic damage alone is not enough.

links.label: NTSB — Report an Accident or Incident

details.summary: Certain incidents require immediate NTSB notification even when they are not accidents. An in-flight fire is one of those listed events. Know the Part 830 incident list separately from the accident definition (death, serious injury, or substantial damage).

Class D airspace around a towered airport is charted for when the tower is operating. When the tower closes, that Class D becomes Class E (or Class G below the shelf, depending on the airspace design). Always check the Chart Supplement for tower hours and the airspace that remains when the tower is closed.

A “commercial operator” is a person who, for compensation or hire, carries persons or property by aircraft in air commerce other than as an air carrier. This definition drives when Part 119 / commercial operating rules apply versus private carriage or personal use.

links.label: 14 CFR Part 119 — Certification: Air Carriers and Commercial Operators

details.summary: V-speeds use standard symbols. VS is the stalling speed or the minimum steady flight speed at which the airplane is controllable. Related marks include VS0 (landing configuration) and VS1 (specified configuration).

For U.S.-registered civil aircraft, an approved Airplane Flight Manual (or Rotorcraft Flight Manual) must be available in the aircraft when required by the type certification. Glider pilots should treat the POH / AFM and placards as the operating limitations source for the specific ship.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.9 — Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements

details.summary: For aerotow, 14 CFR 91.309 requires a safety (weak) link at the glider end with breaking strength not less than 80% and not greater than twice the glider’s maximum certificated operating weight — unless a stronger link is used at the towplane end under the same rule. For a 1,140 lb glider, 80% is 912 lb.

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.309 — Towing: Gliders and unpowered ultralight vehicles
Glider Flying Handbook — Launches and Landing

details.summary: Under 14 CFR 91.211, the required minimum flight crew must use supplemental oxygen for any time exceeding 30 minutes between cabin pressure altitudes of 12,500 and 14,000 feet MSL (inclusive). Above 14,000 feet MSL, the required crew must use oxygen continuously. Passengers have separate requirements above 15,000 feet.

In Class C, D, and E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL, basic VFR minimums are 3 statute miles visibility and cloud clearance of 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 2,000 feet horizontal. At 6,500 feet MSL those values apply unless a different rule (like Class B or special VFR) is in use.

links.label: AIM 3-1-4 — VFR Weather Minimums summary tables

details.summary: Compliance with applicable Airworthiness Directives is the responsibility of the owner or operator of the aircraft. ADs are legally enforceable rules issued under Part 39; they must be accomplished as specified before further flight unless an alternative method of compliance is approved.

The four levels of learning build from lowest to highest: Rote (repeat facts), Understanding (explain concepts), Application (use knowledge to solve problems / perform skills), and Correlation (relate knowledge across domains and adapt in new situations). Instructors should teach toward correlation, not stop at rote memorization.

links.label: AIH PDF — Learning Process / Levels of Learning

details.summary: Introduce aeronautical decision making (ADM) as soon as the student can control the aircraft in basic maneuvers — not after solo, and not delayed until cross-country. Early ADM builds risk awareness while the student still has cognitive bandwidth once basic control is established. Keep ADM practical: identify hazards, assess risk, and mitigate during normal lesson tasks.

links.label: Aviation Instructor’s Handbook — ADM / Risk Management teaching
Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge — Aeronautical Decision-Making

details.summary: Realistic distractions during training flights check whether the student can maintain aircraft control while attention is diverted — a core divide-attention / workload skill. Distractions should be intentional teaching tools (radio calls, checklist interruptions, “passenger” questions), not unsafe overload. The goal is safe control first, then resume the interrupted task.

links.label: Aviation Instructor’s Handbook — Teaching Methods / Flight Instruction

details.summary: Under 14 CFR 61.15, a conviction for any federal or state offense involving the growing, processing, manufacture, sale, disposition, possession, transportation, or importation of narcotic drugs, marijuana, or depressant or stimulant drugs or substances is grounds for suspension or revocation of any certificate, rating, or authorization issued under Part 61. Related alcohol/drug motor vehicle actions also trigger reporting and certificate action rules in 61.15.

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.15 — Offenses involving alcohol or drugs

details.summary: 14 CFR 91.17 prohibits acting or attempting to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft while having a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04 percent or greater by weight. Also barred: within 8 hours after consuming alcohol, while under the influence of alcohol, or while using any drug that affects faculties contrary to safety.

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant that impairs judgment, coordination, and reaction time. It also reduces the body’s tolerance to hypoxia — a given altitude feels “higher” physiologically after drinking. Coffee does not metabolize alcohol faster; only time clears it. Teach the 8-hour bottle-to-throttle rule as a minimum, not a guarantee of fitness.

Spatial disorientation happens when the vestibular and proprioceptive senses conflict with what the eyes see — especially in IMC, night, or unusual attitudes. The recommended recovery is to ignore body sensations and rely entirely on the flight instruments (or a competent safety pilot / instructor on the gauges). Head movement reduction helps avoid vestibular illusions but is not the primary recovery procedure.

Hypoxia symptoms vary by person but commonly include euphoria, belligerence, a false sense of security, impaired judgment, headache, dizziness, tingling, and cyanosis. Nitrogen bubbles cause decompression sickness (the bends), not hypoxia. Concentration alone cannot overcome hypoxia — you need oxygen, lower altitude, or both.

Hypoxic hypoxia at altitude is caused by reduced barometric (atmospheric) pressure, which lowers the partial pressure of oxygen available to the lungs — even though the percentage of oxygen in air stays about 21%. The trap choice “decreasing amount of oxygen with altitude” confuses percentage with partial pressure. Teach students: same mix, less pressure, less O₂ molecules per breath.

Hyperventilation is abnormally rapid or deep breathing that blows off too much carbon dioxide (hypocapnia). Symptoms can mimic hypoxia (dizziness, tingling, visual disturbance). It is a CO₂ problem, not primarily an oxygen shortage — and increasing supplemental oxygen flow is not the fix.

Rapid or overly deep breathing while on oxygen commonly causes hyperventilation. Students may over-breathe when anxious or when first using a mask/cannula. Watch for lightheadedness and tingling; coach calm, normal-rate breathing rather than “more oxygen.”

To overcome hyperventilation: slow the breathing rate and restore carbon dioxide (breathe normally; historically, rebreathing into a paper bag was taught when hypoxia is ruled out). Do not speed up breathing. Distinguish hypoxia (need O₂ / descend) from hyperventilation (need slower breathing / more CO₂).

Smoking (and carbon monoxide exposure) reduces the blood’s oxygen-carrying capability by binding to hemoglobin — a form of hypemic hypoxia. It also degrades night vision. Teach smokers that physiological altitude is effectively higher and that CO plus altitude compounds risk.

For motion sickness in training: have the student minimize unnecessary head movement and keep eyes on a fixed outside reference (horizon). Closing eyes or looking down often worsens it. Avoid recommending medication that is not approved / that impairs performance; many anti-motion-sickness drugs are sedating.

links.label: Aviation Instructor’s Handbook — Student emotional reactions

details.summary: Motion sickness is caused by continued stimulation of the vestibular apparatus in the inner ear (the organs that sense balance and motion), especially when visual and vestibular cues disagree. Experience and smooth instruction help, but the mechanism is vestibular — not stomach acid.

ADM frames every aviation situation with four fundamental risk elements: Pilot, Aircraft, Environment, and External pressures (often taught as mission / external pressures — PAVE: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures). Instructors should have students score each element on every flight.

Altitude-chamber (or similar controlled hypoxia) training’s main advantage is that each pilot learns their own personal hypoxia symptoms in a safe, supervised setting. Symptom sets differ person-to-person; recognizing your pattern early is the teaching point — not merely watching others or relying on rapid chamber repressurization.

links.label: FAA Civil Aerospace Medical Institute (aeromedical education)

details.summary: Hypemic (“anemic”) hypoxia occurs when blood cannot carry enough oxygen — classic classroom example is carbon monoxide from a leaking exhaust system binding to hemoglobin. Symptoms resemble hypoxic hypoxia, but the cause is blood oxygen transport, not low ambient pressure. Treat with fresh air / oxygen and land; fix the exhaust leak on the ground.

FAA definition: Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM) is a systematic approach to the mental process used by pilots to consistently determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances. It is more than “good judgment” alone — it is a structured process (DECIDE plus risk tools like PAVE/CARE).

Risk management within ADM reduces flight risk through situational awareness, problem recognition, and good judgment. Teach students to notice change early (SA), name the problem, then apply sound judgment and mitigation — not just memorize procedures after the fact.

One explicit step in the ADM process is identifying personal attitudes hazardous to safe flight. Before antidotes or DECIDE steps help, the pilot must know which hazardous attitude is driving the poor choice. Build this into debriefs: “Which attitude showed up today?”

Dangerous tendencies / behavior patterns called out in ADM training include peer pressure, get-there-itis / scud running, loss of situational awareness, and operating with inadequate fuel (or energy/options) reserves. Instructors should name these patterns in scenario training and require a mitigation before launch.

Classic hazardous attitudes include antiauthority (“don’t tell me”), impulsivity (“do it quickly”), and resignation (“what’s the use”) — along with macho and invulnerability. Know the five; this question samples three of them. Pair each with its antidote phrase in oral prep.

Hazardous attitudes are counteracted by an appropriate antidotal phrase (e.g., antiauthority → “Follow the rules. They are usually right.”; impulsivity → “Not so fast. Think first.”; invulnerability → “It could happen to me.”; macho → “Taking chances is foolish.”; resignation → “I’m not helpless. I can make a difference.”). Recognition alone is not enough — apply the antidote.

The five hazardous attitudes every pilot faces to some degree: antiauthority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, and resignation. Memorize all five and their antidotes for the FOI/ADM oral and written.

The first step in neutralizing a hazardous attitude is recognizing the hazardous thought when it appears. Only after recognition can the pilot apply the antidote and choose a safer action. Drill recognition in flight debriefs with concrete examples from the lesson.

Cockpit stress management starts before the crisis: assess stress areas in one’s personal life. Life stress carries into the cockpit and reduces spare mental capacity. Instructors should model go/no-go honesty when life stress is high (IMSAFE: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion/Eating).

At the first sign of cockpit stress, relax and think rationally — deliberate calm beats rushing into the next switch or control input. Teach a brief reset: breathe, prioritize aviate/navigate/communicate, then act. Avoid dumping unrelated life-stress analogies into the moment of the emergency.

Bank stem text looks mis-pasted (mentions thermal indices), but the choices/key test dust-devil technique: avoid the clear area at the outside edge of the dust column because of severe downdrafts. Dust marks the rising core; the clear rim is often where air sinks hard. Teach students to treat that clear collar as a no-go, not a “cleaner” entry.

When soaring in a dust devil, an important precaution is to avoid the eye (core) of the vortex because of extreme turbulence. Dust may look inviting as a thermal marker, but the center can be violently turbulent. Prefer the smoother lift on the outside of the rotating column and leave immediately if the ride gets rough.

Wake turbulence wingtip vortices circulate outward, upward, and around each wingtip. From behind the generating airplane, each vortex is a horizontal tornado that sinks and drifts with the wind. Knowing the circulation direction helps you picture where the hazard sits relative to the flightpath.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Departing behind a large jet: minimize wingtip-vortex hazard by becoming airborne before you reach the jet’s flightpath (rotate prior to the jet’s rotation point / liftoff path), then turn clear of the wake. Remaining below the jet’s path keeps you in the sinking vortices; extending the roll past the jet’s rotation point puts you into the vortex trail.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Helicopters in forward flight generate wingtip-like vortices similar to fixed-wing aircraft (plus strong rotor downwash when hovering or at low speed). Do not teach “helicopters only make downwash.” Also remember vortices sink below the generating aircraft’s path after a short time — they do not stay level indefinitely.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Releasing from aerotow while still in the low-tow position risks the tow ring / rope striking and damaging the glider after release (the rope can slap up into the nose or canopy area). Teach normal release from high-tow (or the POH-approved position), confirm clear, then release — and brief abort/rope-break procedures so students never “dive off” low-tow as a habit.

links.label: Glider Flying Handbook — Launches and Landing (Ch 7)

details.summary: Stability is the tendency of an aircraft to develop forces (and moments) that restore it toward its original steady-flight condition after a disturbance. Distinguish static stability (initial tendency) from dynamic stability (behavior over time).

Lift rises with speed largely because relative wind hits the lower surface harder and more air mass is accelerated/deflected downward (Newtonian view). Dynamic pressure also rises with V², so the pressure difference across the wing grows. Same AOA, more speed → more lift — until you hit structural or stall limits.

By definition, lift is the net aerodynamic force perpendicular to the relative wind; drag is parallel to the relative wind. Weight and thrust (or tow force) are separate. Teach students to resolve forces in the relative-wind axes, not the horizon axes, when analyzing climbs and glides.

Angle of incidence is the fixed angle between the wing chord line and the aircraft longitudinal axis — built into the airframe, not changed by the pilot. Do not confuse with angle of attack (chord vs relative wind), which the pilot does change.

Angle of attack (AOA) is the angle between the chord line and the relative wind. AOA — not pitch attitude or airspeed alone — is what the wing “sees.” Stalls occur at a critical AOA regardless of indicated airspeed.

The mean camber line runs from leading edge to trailing edge, equidistant from the upper and lower surfaces. The chord line is the straight line LE→TE. Camber is the curvature between those two lines; more upper camber is typical on glider airfoils.

Bernoulli’s principle (as taught in FAA materials): faster airflow over the curved upper surface lowers static pressure on top of the wing, contributing to lift. Pair this with the downward deflection / Newton explanation — both are part of the complete lift picture.

Wings produce lift from a pressure difference: relatively higher (positive) pressure below and lower (negative) pressure above the wing. That net force is perpendicular to the relative wind. Teach both pressure distribution and downwash as one story.

Induced drag is the drag created as a byproduct of producing lift (wingtip vortices / downwash). It changes strongly with airspeed — roughly inversely with V² in level flight — so it dominates at slow speeds near the stall.
Above L/Dmax speed in level flight, total drag rises mainly because parasite drag increases with speed (≈ V²). Induced drag is falling, but parasite drag grows faster past the L/Dmax “bucket.”

Below L/Dmax speed in level flight, total drag rises because induced drag increases sharply as airspeed drops (higher AOA to hold level flight). That is the backside of the drag curve — important for slow flight and approach energy management.

Profile drag (a form of parasite drag) includes skin friction from air viscosity along the wing surface plus form drag from the airfoil shape. It rises with airspeed and is not the lift-induced component.

Induced drag varies inversely as the square of the airspeed (in steady level flight, roughly). Double the speed → about one-fourth the induced drag. Parasite drag does the opposite — varies with the square of speed.

In a coordinated turn, total lift tilts; the vertical component must still equal weight for level flight. As bank increases, vertical lift decreases unless you increase total lift (back pressure / higher load factor). In a glider, if you do not add enough, you sink faster — bank ↑ → vertical component ↓ → sink rate ↑.

Center of pressure (CP) is where the net aerodynamic force acts on the wing. As CP moves with AOA/configuration changes, pitching moments change — affecting aerodynamic balance and how much control input you need (controllability).

To turn, you must change the direction of lift (bank) so a horizontal component pulls the flightpath around. Rudder alone yaws; elevator alone pitches. A coordinated turn is bank + appropriate pitch + rudder to stay coordinated.

AOA directly controls how pressure is distributed on the wing (upper-surface suction and lower-surface pressure). Change AOA and you change that distribution — and therefore lift, drag, and pitching moment — before airspeed has time to catch up.

links.label: PHAK — Angle of Attack / Pressure Distribution

details.summary: A wing stalls at a critical angle of attack, independent of airspeed. You can stall at high speed (accelerated stall) or low speed — what matters is exceeding critical AOA. Weight, G-load, and CG change the stall speed, not the stalling AOA.

In ground effect, at the same AOA as out of ground effect, lift increases and induced drag decreases because the surface interferes with wingtip vortices / downwash. That is why float on landing happens — the ship “keeps flying” in the cushion.

On the standard total-drag vs airspeed curve (Figure 20), point A at the bottom of the bucket is L/Dmax — maximum lift/drag ratio in steady flight. That speed is the key reference for best glide performance in still air.

On the same drag curve, the airspeed at L/Dmax (often labeled point B depending on the figure edition) gives maximum glide range in still air. Best endurance / minimum sink is a slower speed; do not mix those two up on the oral.

Spiral instability comes from strong static directional stability combined with weak dihedral effect. A small bank → nose yaws into the turn (strong weathercock) → outer wing speeds up → bank steepens into a spiral dive. Dihedral/roll stability is what should fight that.

Positive dynamic stability is the most desirable: after a disturbance, oscillations damp out and the airplane returns to equilibrium. Positive static but negative dynamic means it starts back then oscillates worse — not what you want.

Static instability means that when disturbed from steady flight, the aircraft develops forces that take it farther from the original condition (initial tendency is divergent). Contrast with positive static stability (restoring tendency).

Maneuverability is the quality that lets an aircraft be operated easily and withstand the stresses of flight maneuvers. It is about how readily and safely you can change attitude / flightpath — related to, but not the same as, controllability.

Controllability is the capability of an aircraft to respond to pilot control inputs, especially regarding flightpath and attitude. Soft or heavy controls, CG position, and speed all change how controllable the ship feels.

In a longitudinal phugoid oscillation, airspeed and pitch trade back and forth while angle of attack stays nearly constant. It is a long-period energy exchange (kinetic ↔ potential), not a short-period AOA hunting mode.
Wing dihedral increases lateral (roll) stability: when a wing drops, the lower wing meets the relative wind at a higher AOA and produces more lift, rolling the aircraft back toward wings-level.

Glider airfoils generally have greater camber on the upper surface than the lower surface (positive camber). That shape favors upper-surface acceleration and pressure difference for efficient lift at soaring AOAs.

Maximum gliding distance (still air) occurs at L/Dmax, which is where induced drag equals parasite drag — the bottom of the total-drag curve. Fly that speed (adjusted for wind/sink as needed) for best range.
Best L/D occurs when parasite drag equals induced drag. That identity is the same idea as “bottom of the drag bucket” — useful as a memory hook on the written.

The best L/D ratio itself is essentially constant with weight — a heavy glider flies the same L/Dmax number, but at a higher airspeed. Weight changes the speed for best L/D, not the ratio value (ignoring Reynolds-number nuances).

Cold air is denser: in colder-than-standard temperatures you are lower than the indicated altitude (true altitude < indicated). “From high to low, look out below” applies to both pressure and temperature. Critical for mountain / winter ops.

The oxygen system most commonly found in light GA aircraft is continuous flow (cannula or mask with continuous delivery). Diluter-demand and pressure-demand systems are more typical of higher-performance / high-altitude aircraft.

Density altitude rises when temperature rises, moisture increases, and pressure decreases (hot, humid, low-pressure day = high DA). High DA means less performance: longer ground roll, poorer climb, higher true airspeed for a given IAS.

The Sun is the primary driving force of Earth’s weather — uneven solar heating drives circulation cells, pressure systems, and fronts. Everything else (Coriolis, terrain, moisture) modifies that energy engine.

Bank answer text looks swapped (vortex wording). Concept for the stem: winds at 5,000 feet more southwesterly while surface winds are more southerly mainly because surface friction slows and backs the wind near the ground; above the friction layer the wind is closer to geostrophic / gradient balance.

For a brief summary of fronts, pressure systems, and circulation patterns, use Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) on aviationweather.gov. It replaced many old prog-chart workflows for that quick synoptic picture.

Military training routes with operations at or below 1,500 feet AGL use a four-digit number (IR#### or VR####). Routes mostly above 1,500 feet AGL use three-digit numbers. Charted on IFR/VFR charts — brief them on cross-countries.

Bank answer text looks swapped (takeoff-behind-jet wording). Concept for the stem: a light crosswind (about 5 kt or less) can drift the upwind vortex over the runway and hold it in the touchdown zone longer — so a light crosswind is not “safe,” it can make wake more persistent for the following aircraft.

An aircraft furnished for a practical test must have no prescribed operating limitations that prohibit its use in any required area of operation (and meet the other Part 61 aircraft requirements). If the POH/placards forbid a required task, that ship cannot be used for that checkride task.

A commercial pilot must log the flight time necessary to meet recent flight experience requirements (and other required records). You do not have to log every flight for fun — but you must be able to show currency and qualification when exercising commercial privileges.

Bank answer “24 hours” does not match the stem. Rule: under 14 CFR 91.17, you may not allow a person who appears to be intoxicated / under the influence to be carried in a civil aircraft — except a medical patient under proper care. Teach the passenger alcohol rule separately from the crew 8-hour / 0.04% rules.

Operating limitations are found in the aircraft flight manual / approved manual material, markings, and placards — or any combination thereof (14 CFR 91.9). For gliders, that means POH/AFM pages plus cockpit placards (Vne, weight, weak-link, etc.).

links.label: 14 CFR § 91.9 — Flight manual, marking, and placard requirements

details.summary: Over a congested area, 14 CFR 91.119 requires at least 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a 2,000-foot horizontal radius. Over other than congested areas the minimum is 500 feet AGL (with other caveats). Glider instructors still brief this for aerotow routes and XC.

For a glider above 10,000 feet MSL and more than 1,200 feet AGL, basic VFR visibility minimum is 5 SM (with 1,000 ft above / 1,000 ft below / 1 SM horizontal cloud clearance). Below those altitudes different Class E/G tables apply — know § 91.155.

Acrobatic flight minimums under 14 CFR 91.303 include at least 1,500 feet AGL and 3 statute miles visibility (plus the other listed restrictions: not over congested areas, not in Class B/C/D/E surface areas without authorization, etc.).

Each occupant must wear an approved parachute when an intentional maneuver exceeds 30° nose-up or nose-down relative to the horizon (with the usual training/spin exceptions in 91.307). Brief this before intentional unusual-attitude demos.

If an alteration or repair substantially affected flight operation, the aircraft records must show a test flight and approval for return to service by an appropriately rated pilot before passengers are carried (14 CFR 91.407). Maintenance signoff alone is not enough when ops were substantially affected.

Haze makes traffic and terrain appear farther away than they really are — so you can be closer than your eyes suggest. Teach students to slow the scan assumptions and use ADS-B/radio as backups, not substitutes for seeing.

Teach a systematic empty-field scan: focus on different segments of the sky for short intervals rather than staring or continuously sweeping without focusing. Eyes need a moment to focus at each point to detect traffic.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: At night, rods (off-center vision) detect dim objects better than cones (center). Force off-center viewing — look slightly to the side of where you expect the target — to increase night vision effectiveness.

Most effective night traffic technique: avoid staring directly at the suspected aircraft — use peripheral / off-center vision and a scanning pattern. Staring bleaches night vision on that spot and can make the target disappear.

Classic behavioral traps for experienced pilots: complete the flight as planned, please passengers, meet schedules, and “get the job done.” Call these out in ADM scenario training — mission completion pressure is a leading human-factor hazard.

To get a realistic view of your attitude toward flying, take a Self-Assessment Hazardous Attitude Inventory Test (FAA ADM materials). It surfaces which of the five hazardous attitudes you lean toward so you can practice antidotes.

When you recognize a hazardous thought: label it as hazardous, then correct it by stating the corresponding antidotal phrase — and act on the antidote. Recognition without the antidote leaves the bad attitude in charge.

VOR/OMNI figure item: indication V2 corresponds to aircraft position 2 only. Mentally place the OBS/TO-FROM and CDI: match the depicted needle/flag to the position on the radial/arc. Practice with the actual knowledge-test figure.
VOR/OMNI figure item: indication U corresponds to aircraft position 6 only. Same method — resolve OBS setting, TO/FROM, and CDI deflection against each numbered position until only one fits.

VOR/OMNI figure item: aircraft 8 would show indication W. Work TO/FROM and left/right sensing from the aircraft’s position relative to the selected course; W is the unique match for that station geometry.

Bank answer text looks swapped (airfoil axis wording). Concept for the stem: on older radar summary charts, an echo top like .250 with an underline coded the maximum top height band (tens of thousands of feet). Prefer modern GFA / radar mosaics on aviationweather.gov for current products, and learn the legend of whatever chart the test figure shows.

Human behavior is cited as a factor in about three out of four accidents — the teaching point behind ADM, CRM, and risk management. Technical skill matters, but judgment and behavior dominate the accident record.

A forecast K-index of 35 implies a high likelihood of thunderstorms (commonly taught as about a 60% chance in FAA weather materials). Higher K → more unstable / moist mid-levels → better thunderstorm potential. Cross-check with outlooks, radar, and AIRMETs/SIGMETs.

Extending flaps increases wing camber, which increases both lift and drag (for a given AOA/speed regime). That is why flaps allow slower approach speeds but also steeper approaches / more drag for path control.
Same key idea as the other stability card: the most desirable stability is positive dynamic stability — disturbances damp out over time and the aircraft returns to equilibrium.

Gliders usually feel ground effect at less than about half the wingspan above the surface. Long-span ships therefore enter ground effect higher than short-span trainers — plan the roundout accordingly to avoid prolonged float.

Induced drag is the portion of total drag created by producing lift, and it changes a lot with airspeed (high at low speed). Duplicate of the core induced-drag teaching point — hammer it for the oral.
Lift is the net force perpendicular to the relative wind — same definition card as bank_009. Keep drag parallel to relative wind; do not measure lift off the horizon.

Adverse yaw on turn entry comes from aileron drag: the raised wing’s down-aileron makes more lift and more induced drag, while the lowered wing’s up-aileron makes less lift and less induced drag — so the nose yaws opposite the roll. Teach coordinated rudder with aileron from the start of the roll.

Rolling out of a steep turn, the lowered aileron (on the rising wing) creates more drag than on roll-in because the wing’s angle of attack is higher at rollout start (you are still loaded up). That extra AOA amplifies aileron drag — another reason for firm coordinating rudder on rollout.

Positive static stability (longitudinal): after you push the elevator forward and release, the nose initially tends to return toward the original pitch attitude. Initial restoring tendency = positive static stability.

Negative static stability: after a pitch disturbance (elevator forward and release), the nose initially moves farther from the original position. Divergent initial tendency — undesirable for a training glider.
Neutral static stability: after elevator forward and release, the nose stays at the new attitude — no restoring and no divergent tendency. Contrast with positive (returns) and negative (keeps going).

A slight upward (negative) flap deflection reduces camber and typically decreases drag — used on some sailplanes for high-speed cruise / interthermal runs. Down flaps increase camber, lift, and drag for thermaling or landing.

In a turn, the inward (horizontal) component of lift is opposed by centrifugal force. In a steady coordinated turn those horizontal forces balance; lift’s vertical component balances weight (level turn) or not (climbing/descending turn).

Nose swings left before going right on a right-turn entry = slipping entry: not enough right rudder for the aileron used. Fix: more rudder with the aileron so the nose tracks with the horizon into the turn (coordinated).

If the nose moves into the turn before the bank starts, rudder was applied too soon (or too much) relative to aileron. Teach simultaneous coordinated inputs: aileron + rudder together, not rudder leading the roll.
Nose-low in a steep turn: reduce bank first, then apply back elevator to restore pitch. Pulling first while steep only increases load factor and can accelerate the spiral / stall. Bank → then pitch.

Straight-and-level in a crosswind: establish a proper heading into the wind (crab) with coordinated controls — wings level, ball centered, heading that cancels drift. Do not hold aileron into the wind for cruise crab (that’s a slip).

A slipping turn is likely when you increase the rate of turn without using rudder (or with insufficient rudder) — bank/turn rate ahead of yaw coordination. Ball goes to the inside; fix with rudder toward the ball / less bank.
The three aircraft axes (longitudinal, lateral, vertical) intersect at the center of gravity. Moments and stability are referenced to that CG point — which is why loading changes handling.

Center of pressure is the point on the airfoil through which the net aerodynamic lift (pressure force) acts. It moves with AOA and is not the same as CG — the relationship between CP and CG drives pitching moments.

Critical (stalling) angle of attack depends on wing design (airfoil, planform, devices) — not on weight or airspeed. Weight and CG change stall speed; they do not change the stalling AOA of that wing configuration.
CG is computed along the longitudinal axis (fore-aft station). Lateral imbalance matters operationally, but standard W&B worksheets solve for the longitudinal CG location in inches from datum.

links.label: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook

details.summary: CG = total moment ÷ total weight. Moment is weight × arm. Add all weights and all moments, then divide. Same formula for gliders with pilot, ballast, and optional water.

links.label: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook

details.summary: Highest stalling speed occurs with high gross weight and a forward CG. Heavy + forward CG means you need more lift (higher AOA sooner / higher speed) and the wing/tail combo stalls at a higher IAS.

Moving CG from aft limit to beyond the forward limit decreases cruising speed and increases stalling speed. Forward CG means more download on the tail (more trim drag) and a higher stall speed — sluggish and nose-heavy.

details.summary: Exceeding the forward CG limit produces higher stalling speeds and more longitudinal stability (very stable but heavy elevator, hard flare). Aft of limits does the opposite: lower stall speed feel, less stability, easier to stall/spin.

Water ballast: keep it while thermals are strong so higher wing loading gives higher interthermal cruise speed; dump when thermals weaken so you can thermal efficiently at a lower wing loading / lower sink. Net goal: increase average cross-country speed.

details.summary: If equipment has been added beyond original empty weight, allowable useful load decreases (max gross − new empty weight). Always use current empty weight/CG from the latest W&B sheet, not the old POH sample empty weight.

details.summary: Northern Hemisphere magnetic compass: acceleration on east or west headings makes the compass indicate a turn toward the north (ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South). Use this when teaching compass errors on climb/descent entries.
Acceleration/deceleration errors are negligible on north or south headings — the compass indicates correctly while speeding up or slowing down on N/S. Errors show on E/W headings (ANDS).

Magnetic deviation is compass error from local magnetic fields in the aircraft — metals, electronics, speakers, etc. It is unique to each airplane/installation and is corrected with a compass correction card.

Rolling out to south with a magnetic compass (Northern Hemisphere): start rollout after the compass passes south by about (latitude − normal rollout lead) degrees. Southerly turns are lead/lag reversed from northerly turns — overshoot south, undershoot north.

From a south heading, rolling into a standard-rate right turn (Northern Hemisphere): the compass indicates a turn to the right but faster than the actual turn (leads). UNOS memory aid: Undershoot North, Overshoot South when rolling out.
Deviation varies with heading on the same aircraft — that is why the compass card lists corrections by heading blocks. Variation is geographic; deviation is airframe/heading-dependent.

Measure true course on a sectional at a meridian near mid-route because meridians converge: the angle between your course and true north changes along the route. Midpoint measurement averages that convergence error.
Wind triangle (typical FAA figure): the line from A to B represents true heading and airspeed (the aircraft vector through the air). Know which leg is TH/AS vs TC/GS vs wind.
Wind triangle: line from C to B represents groundspeed and true course (the path over the ground). That is the course/GS vector you plot on the chart.
Wind triangle: line from C to A represents wind direction and velocity (from wind-dot to air-vector tip, depending on construction). Wind is from → to along that vector.

True course → magnetic heading: apply variation (add west / subtract east — “East is least, West is best”), then apply wind correction (subtract left WCA / add right WCA) to get magnetic heading. Sequence: TC ± var = MC, then ± WCA = MH.
Magnetic course → true course: add easterly variation (and subtract westerly). Going MC→TC is the reverse of TC→MC. Variation depends on location, not on which way the nose is pointed.
True heading → true course: remove the wind correction angle — subtract a right WCA (or add a left WCA). Heading is where the nose points; course is the path over the ground.
Magnetic variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north. It is printed on charts as isogonic lines and changes slowly over years — always use current chart variation.
